title: Mastering Medial Entropion: From Pathophysiology to Surgical Reconstruction
summary: Medial entropion of the lower eyelid is a common, often under-diagnosed cause of chronic ocular surface irritation. This guide covers the surgical management and biomechanical principles required for definitive correction.

sections.title: Clinical Definition
sections.content: Medial entropion is an inward rotation of the medial portion of the eyelid margin, often involving the punctum. It leads to trichiasis (cilia rubbing the globe) and often epiphora due to punctal malposition or canalicular kinking.

rows: Extra row of lashes from Meibomian glands

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Refer
content: Acute onset with facial nerve palsy
Signs of chemical injury or cicatrizing conjunctivitis

sections.title: Surgical Management Algorithm
content: Step 1: Diagnostic 'Snap-Back' test to assess horizontal laxity.
Step 2: Medial spindle procedure for mild cases; subciliary incision with excision of medial tarsal strip.
Step 3: Tightening of the medial canthal tendon if dehiscence is present.
Step 4: Orbicularis orbicularis oculi muscle stripping to prevent override.
Step 5: 6-0 Vicryl suture closure for conjunctival and tarsal defects.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always evaluate for punctal stenosis before committing to surgical correction.
The 'snap-back' test is the gold standard for quantifying horizontal lid laxity.
Medial entropion is rarely isolated; check for global lid laxity.
Post-operative lubrication is vital to prevent corneal exposure during healing.
If recurrence happens, consider underlying cicatricial diseases like OCP or SJS.
